newsitem.title: ANTARCTICA: FEATURE-Wild Antarctic waters are a challenge.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Wild Antarctic waters are a challenge.

text.p: Waves crash over the bow, the sky is a furious gray and the ship rolls and creaks with every ocean swell. But for Capt. Karl Sanden of the Polar Duke, it is a blessedly quiet day in the Drake Passage.

"You never know what you're going to get here," he said, shifting his weight from side to side to keep his balance as the ship heaved to port and starboard. "You can get caught in a storm, or you can get locked in ice. You can take a wrong turn and hit a seamount. You have currents from the west, currents from the east, the flow can go in any direction.
"In the winter, it's dark all the time and you've got to worry about icebergs. Sometimes the maps aren't so good either," he said.

Sanden has skippered ships in the Arctic near his native Norway, in the North Sea and in plenty of other famously dangerous bodies of water. But none, he says, are quite as nasty as the Drake Passage, which separates Antarctica and South America at the only place where the world's two largest oceans meet in a chaos of currents, winds and storms that can test the nerves -- or the sanity -- of even the most experienced captain.
ENOUGH TO MAKE LIVING WISH THEY WERE DEAD

"The Drake is enough to make the living wish they were dead. It's enough to make an atheist believe in God," said Patricio Rojas, the Polar Duke's cook, who says he has endured it more times than he cares to remember.

With more tour ships heading for Antarctica from Chile or Argentina, plus the usual flow of yachtsmen, the Drake Passage is getting busier. And the captains of those ships had better be prepared for what awaits them, veterans say.

"You're in a vortex here because it's between two oceans. The water is not terribly deep, it's just the weather that makes it so dangerous," Alan Hickey, a Massachusetts-born seaman and organiser of scientific programmes on the Norwegian-flagged Polar Duke, said.

The ship, whose bright orange hull stands out like a flame, is used by the U.S. National Science Foundation to ferry staff and supplies between Antarctica and Punta Arenas, Chile. Once, on the Antarctic side of the passage a few years ago, it was caught by ice and stopped dead in its tracks for 14 days, Sanden said. Fortunately the ship had plenty of food.
"An American icebreaker had to come cut a path for us so we could get out. When we returned to Chile, we saw that it was all written up in the newspapers," he said with a grin.

Others have not been so lucky. Canadian sailor Gerry Roufs' yacht was last heard from somewhere west of Cape Horn in mid-January as he approached the passage during the Vendee Globe round-the-world race.

The Drake Passage is so wild because it lies at the only latitude outside the Arctic with no major land mass. Wind swirls around the globe with nothing to stop it, squeezed between Antarctica and South America like pincers.

The circular currents act as a barrier between Antarctica and the rest of the world. "They isolate Antarctica, cut it off it from the rest the world, and that's why its wildlife is unique. There are no sharks in Antarctica, for example, and krill exists only in Antarctica," U.S. oceanographer David Karl said.
HELP IS NOT ON THE WAY
Hurricane-force winds are common in the Drake Passage, 30-foot (9 metre)-high waves can smother a ship, and, unless you are near the Argentine or Chilean coasts, help could be days away.

"What makes this place so treacherous is that there is not much shipping or commercial fishing," Gary Osborne, a crewman from Oregon, said. "In Alaska you're never more than 30 minutes away from a rescue. Down here, if you've got an emergency, you're stuck. Once you leave the southern tip of South America, you're on your own."

Modern radar has made navigation much safer than only 10 years ago but disaster still awaits those who are unwary, unprepared or simply unlucky. In 1989, the Argentine tour ship Bahia Paraiso struck rocks off Anvers Island, Antarctica. All 150 people were safely evacuated but the fuel tanks ruptured and 600 tonnes of diesel oil gushed into the ocean. The ship later capsized in a storm and still lies there, belly up.
A month later, a Peruvian naval ship, the Humboldt, blew onto the rocks near King George's Island and caused another oil spill. It was refloated with the help of the Chilean navy.

"There's more traffic these days around the Antarctic Peninsula, more people coming down," Sanden said. "If they're going to be in this area, they better have ice-strength hulls and they better know what they're doing."
